questions.title: How does the DPO objective recover the optimal KL‑constrained policy without estimating the partition function?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 the paper derives Eq. (4) from the optimal policy form in Eq. (3) and then substitutes this into the Bradley‑Terry model to obtain Eq. (5). The authors claim that the partition function \(Z(x)\) cancels out, yielding a preference probability that depends only on the ratios \(\pi^*(y\mid x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\). I am unsure how this cancellation works algebraically, especially since \(Z(x)\) appears inside a logarithm in Eq. (4). Could someone walk through the step‑by‑step algebra showing the cancellation, and explain why no approximation of \(Z(x)\) is needed in practice?

questions.title: Why does the DPO loss weight examples by \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\) and how does this prevent degeneration?
questions.question_body: Equation (7) shows the gradient of the DPO loss, where the term \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x, y_w))\) acts as a weight. The authors state that without this weighting the model collapses (see Appendix Table X). I would like to understand intuitively why weighting by the sigmoid of the reward difference is necessary and how it discourages the model from assigning high probability to dispreferred completions. How does this compare to the unlikelihood loss term used in the "Unlikelihood" baseline?

questions.title: What is the equivalence class of reward functions and why does it not affect the optimal policy?
questions.question_body: The paper defines two reward functions as equivalent if they differ by a function \(f(x)\) that depends only on the prompt. Lemma 2 claims that reward functions in the same class induce the same optimal policy under the KL‑constrained objective. I am confused because adding a constant (or prompt‑dependent) offset changes the absolute values of rewards. How does the KL constraint make these offsets irrelevant, and could anyone provide a short proof or intuition for Lemma 2?

questions.title: How is the reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) chosen when an SFT model is unavailable, and what impact does this have on DPO performance?
questions.question_body: Section 4 mentions that if a supervised‑fine‑tuned (SFT) model is not present, \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is obtained by maximum likelihood on the preferred completions. Does this choice guarantee that \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is close enough to the true data distribution for the KL‑penalty to be meaningful? Have the authors evaluated the sensitivity of DPO to a mismatched reference policy, and what practical guidelines should be followed when constructing \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)?

questions.title: Why does PPO‑GT sometimes outperform standard PPO even though both optimize the same KL‑constrained objective?
questions.question_body: In the controlled sentiment experiment, the authors include PPO‑GT (PPO with ground‑truth rewards) and report that DPO still dominates it. However, PPO‑GT sometimes yields a better reward‑KL trade‑off than vanilla PPO. What modifications are made in PPO‑GT (e.g., reward normalization, advantage estimation) that give it an edge, and could these ideas be incorporated into standard PPO to close the gap with DPO?

questions.title: How does DPO handle the combinatorial explosion of possible completions when computing the loss over a batch of preference pairs?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss in Eq. (6) requires evaluating \(\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\) and \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\) for both the winner and loser completions of each pair. In practice, do we need to enumerate all tokens of each completion, and does this incur a large computational overhead compared to PPO which samples trajectories? How is this implemented efficiently for large models (e.g., 6B parameters) and long sequences?

questions.title: Can the DPO framework be extended to multi‑turn dialogues or ranking more than two candidates?
questions.question_body: The current derivation relies on the binary Bradley‑Terry model. For tasks like multi‑turn conversation or when we have a ranked list of >2 completions (e.g., Plackett‑Luce), how would the DPO objective change? Is there a straightforward generalization, or does the closed‑form policy reparameterization break down when moving beyond pairwise comparisons?

questions.title: What is the role of the temperature‑like hyperparameter \(\beta\) in DPO, and how should it be tuned?
questions.question_body: The paper treats \(\beta\) as a KL‑constraint strength, analogous to the PPO KL‑penalty coefficient. In experiments they sweep over \(\beta\in\{0.05,0.1,1,5\}\). How does changing \(\beta\) affect the implicit reward (Eq. 7) and the resulting policy’s conservativeness? Is there a principled way (e.g., target KL) to select \(\beta\) instead of brute‑force grid search?

questions.title: Why does the "Best of N" baseline sometimes outperform PPO and DPO, and is this a fair comparison?
questions.question_body: The authors report that sampling many candidates from the SFT model and picking the highest‑scoring one (according to a learned reward) can beat PPO and DPO, yet it is computationally impractical. Does this indicate that the reward model is still useful for ranking, and could DPO be combined with a sampling‑and‑ranking step to further improve performance? How should we interpret the "Best of N" results when evaluating alignment methods?
